A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HAM research, despite the changed title and organization. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original linear-regression simulations and experiments on vision, LLM fine-tuning, graph classification and node classification in Section 6 and Appendix D.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds mechanism measurements, component ablations, sparse-transformer results and mask/pruning experiments in Section 5 and Appendices F–G.

M1.justification: The deployed optimizer step followed by HYP*, reusing the gradient and using the updated parameter sign, remains unchanged. The clipping disclosure and layerwise-alpha toy analysis do not establish a revision to the deployed method.

E1.justification: Both evaluate Gaussian linear regression, ImageNet, CIFAR100, eight commonsense tasks, four graph benchmarks and thirteen node benchmarks. The new sparse-DeiT and mask experiments change model or training configurations within retained coverage. LLM and graph results are relocated, not removed.

E2.justification: V2 adds RiGL + Sign-In to the sparsification comparison, HYP-only to the regression comparison, and evaluated SNIP/Synflow mask sources. V1's dense m⊙w training-loss comparison disappears, although m⊙w participates in the new inverse-metric analysis. Most existing comparator sets remain.

E3.justification: V2 introduces controlled wrong-sign initialization and alpha/learning-rate sweeps, fixed-mask retraining, posttraining magnitude pruning, and 50%-sparse DeiT training. It also changes the reported regression learning rate from 10e-4 to 10^-4 and DeiT's from 0.001 to 0.005. These reported revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses directly measure sign flips and inverse-metric trajectories, isolate the two update components, test recovery as alpha increases, compare fixed mask topologies, and examine pruning tolerance (Figure 2a, Appendices F and G.1/G.4/G.5). Existing hyperparameter and negative-alpha analyses remain; the earlier dense m⊙w loss analysis is removed.

E5.justification: The existing three-seed vision/graph summaries, single-seed hyperparameter searches and node-classification reporting practices remain. V2 Table 10 newly identifies SNIP baseline and Sign-In scores as single surviving runs because other seeds crashed. Changed DeiT uncertainty values alone do not establish a changed statistical procedure.

E6.justification: V2 adds mechanism, mask, pruning and sparse-DeiT results; Table 9 reports 73.24 ± 0.45 with HAM versus 72.50 ± 0.16 without. New RiGL + Sign-In exceeds RiGL + HAM at 95% sparsity, 73.07 versus 72.93. Dense-DeiT HAM changes from 72.65 ± 0.09 to 72.62 ± 0.22 alongside a revised reported learning rate. Most existing benchmark scores remain, while the m⊙w 76.56% result disappears.

T1.justification: V2 replaces the eventual sign-stability assumption with a flow-equivalence argument for nonzero initialization (Theorem B.6). It adds nonzero-beta regularized-objective analysis and a one-neuron sign-flip theorem, revises PL convergence bounds, and corrects the Fisher-information definition. These substantially extend and revise the mathematical treatment.

C1.justification: Both claim that HAM provides a lightweight, optimizer-compatible hyperbolic step that avoids near-zero slowdown, controls sparsity bias, improves dense and sparse generalization, and complements SAM. V2 foregrounds sparsity and sign flips, but retains the broader applicability claims and supporting experiments.

C2.justification: V2 explains acceleration away from zero after sign correction and develops the distinct effects of alpha and beta. Appendix B.1 newly qualifies implicit-bias optimality as requiring regularization to be switched off. The added mask discussion identifies SNIP failure and proposes trainability and layerwise sparsity ratios as explanations for topology-dependent performance.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents exponent clipping to [-5, 5], the original regression experiment's alpha value, transformer HAM settings and the TurboPrune implementation basis. It adds a reproducibility statement saying experimental code is attached; availability cannot be verified from the supplied PDFs. These are disclosures rather than demonstrated implementation changes.

R1.justification: V2 adds references including Bernstein et al. on multiplicative updates, Jin et al. on pruning/generalization, Sun et al. on mirror descent, classical alternating/proximal methods, and TurboPrune. Comparisons with exponential and alternating optimization expand, while the principal positioning relative to PILoT, Sign-In and mirror flow remains.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and substantial explanatory passages are rewritten, and 'artificial learning rate' becomes 'inverse metric' throughout. The algorithm moves before the theory, natural-gradient interpretation moves into the appendix, and experimental and appendix sections are substantially reorganized around sparsity and mechanisms.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes from a three-dimensional surface display to a two-dimensional annotated plot, and Figure 2a replaces training loss with sign-flip trajectories. V2 adds a comparison table, explanatory diagrams and experimental displays. The main dense-results table is condensed while its full ablation table and the LLM/graph tables appear in the appendix.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, direct mechanism measurements, component and mask tests, failure reporting and clipping disclosure strengthen empirical support and reproducibility. However, the new Theorem E.2 proof defines its invariant region by a < -w, w > 0, then incorrectly places a = w > 0 inside it. This internal inconsistency limits the theoretical gain, leaving a modest net improvement despite the substantial revision.
